Oath & ActionBrand Guide, Edition 06 · Phase 2 · Atlas visual system

Board 1 of the atlas concepts · October 30, 2026

The frame and the ideas

Four specialists set the rules every concept will share, and a designer who saw none of the earlier work pitched ten ways to draw the system from scratch. This board shows both, with the data visualization research you asked for. The twelve concepts get built after your answers.

What you are asked

  1. Pick the six concepts from scratch (sections 1 and 3). The studio recommends the ideation agent's six with one swap: Editorial Desk, a newspaper-graphics treatment shaped by your note on the Times, in place of Honeycomb.
  2. Approve the shared frame as a set (section 2): the four levels and their reading rules, loops drawn as routes, the navigation model, and the type and line scale.
  3. Say when the data visualization system starts (section 4). Recommended: right after you pick an atlas direction, so charts and maps share one visual language with the atlas.

A reply can be this short: "Six: as recommended. Frame: approved. Data viz: after the atlas pick."

12, option B · Recommended

Editorial Desk

White No sketch yet

The system drawn the way a newspaper graphics desk would draw it. The route the headline names runs in Charcoal and everything else sits back in Stone. Notes are set inside the drawing on fine leaders, the title is a sentence that states the finding, and the steps of R10 are told in order as the reader scrolls.

Its structure is the data visualization lead's plan: the core areas as a ring with printed counts, and the 23 loops as the way in. Its look comes from the research in section 4, direction A, Annotated Newsprint. No other concept takes on the style you named.

02

The shared frame

Every concept follows these rules, so the twelve differ in their big idea and meet one standard of finish. Each part comes from a specialist's memo in work/handoffs/phase-2/.

The reader and the four levels

Civic education expert · 20261030_Atlas-Civic-Education-Memo.md

LevelThe one question it answersWhat a reader leaves with
The systemWhat shapes who officials answer to?Conditions push on one another, and 23 chains of cause return to where they started.
Area CCan officials here lose their seats, and who controls election rules?Electoral pressure (C3) is where R10 and B4 meet. B4 works only where seats are competitive, and R10 makes seats safe.
Loop R10Why does a safe-seat official answer to a small primary electorate, and why does that last?Each turn feeds the next, and the weakest step, L53, is plausible.
Reform R-01What would R-01 change, and who could adopt it?It acts on three named points, L08, L25 and C2, and each outcome family is rated on its own, never totaled.

Three rules the expert ranks first

  • Print "raises" or "lowers" on every connection a first-time reader meets, and keep the plus and minus signs beside the words. A newcomer reads the plus between housing scarcity and owner home equity (L38) as "scarcity is good."
  • Build each loop's read-aloud line from its signs by script. For R10: "More safe seats, more primary decisiveness, less electoral pressure, more incumbent control of election rules, and back to more safe seats."
  • Show each loop's weakest step and its reforms on the loop's own view, so a loop never reads as fate. 22 of the 23 loops have at least one reform (B5 has none).

Draft overview lines, written by the studio

Who do officials answer to?

This map links 51 conditions, from household wealth to court rulings, through 118 connections. Each connection carries a grade for the strength of its evidence.

Can your representative lose their seat?

"In a safe seat, the primary decides who wins, and few people vote in it." That pattern is one of 23 loops on this map of 51 conditions and the connections between them.

Where economic power meets public office.

The map follows 118 connections among 51 conditions, from household wealth to the risk of losing office. In 23 places, a chain of causes returns to where it started.

How to read the map, in 23 words: "Each name is a condition that can rise or fall; an arrow shows one raising or lowering another. Broken lines mark weaker evidence."

Loops drawn as their own routes

Data visualization lead · 20261030_Atlas-Dataviz-Memo.md, shared/20261030_Loop-Route-Thumbnails-Study.html

23loops, 20 with a complete numbered chain
0.57highest similarity of any two thumbnails, under the 0.60 limit (R1 and R6)
310pixels wide for the full form; below 256 px a thumbnail is a locator only
  • The plan puts the outside drivers on top, the economy and technology layers below, and the five core areas in a ring between them. The core's 38 connections between areas join only seven pairs, so in the ring every one joins two neighbors.
  • Each step carries its evidence texture, a pointing tag for sign and direction, and a bar on the step that closes the loop. Sketched loops (B2, B3, R9) sit off the map and say so.
  • Its overview advice: draw all 118 connections and you get 339 crossings. Draw the ring with the seven core counts printed as numbers and you get none, with the 23 loops as the way in and every connection one click down.
  • Each concept may draw its thumbnails in its own style, as the ten sketches do, as long as each one is the loop's real route (DR-15).

Moving between levels

UX and accessibility lead · 20261030_Atlas-Interaction-Memo.md, shared/atlas-kit.js, shared/20261030_Atlas-Kit-Demo.html

  • Views with a panel. Each level has its own address (overview, area C, loop R10), so the Back button always moves up a level. An area or loop opens with a short zoom from the item clicked. A variable, connection or reform opens in a side panel, which becomes a bottom sheet on a phone.
  • Hover never carries anything that focus and tap do not also give. Arrow keys move along the drawing, and every drawing has its lines in words.
  • A loop can be stepped through one link at a time, with play, pause and reset, and a still sequence for readers who turn motion off.
  • Tested: 76 scripted checks pass, and axe-core finds 0 violations in nine states.

Type, lines and grounds

Design director · 20261030_Atlas-Design-Frame-Memo.md, shared/20261030_Atlas-Type-And-Line-Specimen.html

  • Type scale. Display in Inter Tight 800 at 56 px, headline 40, panel head 22; deck in Inter at 19, body 17; station labels in Inter Tight 700 at 20, map labels in Inter 600 at 15; notes, legends and source lines at 13; quotes in Lora Italic at 22; and the two-part ID chip.
  • One stroke family of 1, 1.5, 2, 3 and 6 px, with each evidence pattern drawn in multiples of its line width so a texture keeps its shape from the overview to the lit route.
  • One arrowhead sized by weight. Labels stay 4 px clear of every stroke.
  • One working red per view. Red never marks a sign, a hover state or navigation, and never sits on Prussian.
  • Faults on the generated boards that no concept copies: redrawn wordmarks, five to ten reds in a view, renamed variables and reforms, steps without signs, tints outside the palette.

Calls the studio made today

  • D2-56: the pointing tag is the default sign mark in every concept. Choice 3 of the direction review stays open for you.
  • D2-57: inside a dense map, a node may print its bare code (C1) when the key names the type.
  • D2-58: until you decide P3, the current icon in a row keeps its red as the view's working red.
  • D2-59: Dim Newsprint, adopted at Gate 1, joins the atlas palette for secondary text on dark grounds.
  • D2-60: one stroke family for every atlas drawing.

04

Data visualization research

You asked for an Oath & Action system for charts, graphs, maps and tables, with the Times as the style you like most. The research lead read the four sites you sent, plus Our World in Data, which the brief requires. The full brief is work/research/20261030_Data-Viz-System-References.md, with 28 rules and 13 study captures.

Read

  • The Gagnier case study, including four Times brand principles
  • The Times's open-source ai2html tool and a 2016 talk by Archie Tse, then a Times graphics director
  • Public writing by three Times graphics editors, and five Times charts reproduced on Datawrapper's blog
  • Ten Carbon data visualization pages
  • BBC GEL's infographic and chart description guidance, and the BBC's bbplot package and its R cookbook
  • Our World in Data's redesign article and a live chart, map and table
  • The Economist's 2017 map style guide

Not read

  • Any nytimes.com page. The site refuses automated requests, and the studio respects that. How Times charts behave on phones, and its small multiples, tables and source lines, stay unverified.
  • The Economist's 2017 chart guide, which is no longer online, and one article that refused the connection
  • Carbon's chart accessibility page, which returns an error

If you save a few Times graphics pages as PDFs or screenshots, the studio can study the Times first hand.

Five rules the research lead ranks first

  • The title is a sentence that states the finding, with its evidence kind (finding, association, estimate, illustration) as a label above it.
  • Annotation goes inside the chart, on fine leader lines.
  • Context data in Stone, the series the title names in Charcoal.
  • Red marks only the one point the headline names, and never a series or a scale.
  • Diverging scales never pair red with blue. Two candidates to test at Gate 2: Stone to Verdigris, and Prussian through Newsprint to Verdigris.

Three candidate directions

A. Annotated Newsprint

Times-style sentence titles and annotation on Newsprint, with our evidence labels and grade-matched verbs.

B. Field Instrument

Hairline technical charts on the Signal Grid, labeled with real Atlas V7 IDs.

C. Two-Ink Register

Prussian and Verdigris only, with tables as first-class views and chart, table and map tabs.

Decisions

  1. The six concepts from scratch. Options: the ideation agent's six (Great Circle, Star Atlas, Open Atlas, Kitchen Table, Flywheels and Governors, Honeycomb); the same with Editorial Desk in place of Honeycomb; or your own picks from the ten.Recommended: Editorial Desk in place of Honeycomb. It tests the newspaper style you named, and Honeycomb overlaps concept 04.
  2. The shared frame, as a set. The four levels and the reading rules, loops drawn as routes, views with a panel, and the type, line and ground rules, with the calls D2-56 to D2-60.Recommended: approve as a set.
  3. When the data visualization system starts. Options: (a) in Phase 3 order, after the atlas, the open direction review items and Gate 2; (b) right after you pick an atlas direction.Recommended: (b). Charts, maps and the atlas share type, lines and color, so building them together keeps one language.

After your answers, twelve makers build in parallel, each concept passes the shared checks, the creative director scores all twelve, and Board 2 shows them at true size with a recommendation of two or three.
